extracted.intended_audience: jurors, trial judges, and litigators in U.S. design patent cases
extracted.subtask_description: Model jury instructions and legal standards for evaluating design patent issues at trial, including claim construction, infringement (direct/indirect/contributory/willful), and invalidity (anticipation, public use, on-sale, prior design, obviousness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary of patent issues to decide
rubrics_metrics.description: The jury must decide (1) whether the plaintiff has proved that the defendant infringed the patent, (2) whether the defendant has proved that the patent is invalid, and (3) what amount of damages, if any, the plaintiff has proved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List any other patent issues in the particular case as needed. (Page 19-20)

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction — judge defines claim meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: It is the judge’s job to provide the meaning of the claim of the asserted design patent(s); the jury must accept and use the judge’s meaning in deciding infringement and invalidity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The design patent claim states it covers the design “as shown and described.” Figures/drawings define the boundaries of the claimed design. (Page 21-22)

rubrics_metrics.name: Single claim and multiple embodiments
rubrics_metrics.description: A design patent can only have one claim; multiple embodiments may be illustrated in a single application only if they are directed to substantially the same design and are not patentably distinct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge may instruct whether multiple embodiments are present and whether they are patentably distinct. (Page 21)

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of claimed design — overall visual appearance
rubrics_metrics.description: The scope of the claim encompasses the design’s visual appearance as a whole and the visual impression it creates; do not cover a broad general design concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider all figures in the patent and all visual features of the design as a whole rather than isolated portions. (Page 22)

rubrics_metrics.name: Solid lines vs broken lines in drawings
rubrics_metrics.description: All matter depicted in solid lines contributes to the overall appearance of the design and is part of the claim; features shown in broken lines and described as disclaimed are excluded from the claimed design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to show features in broken lines signals inclusion of such features in the claimed design. Functional features illustrated in solid lines are part of the claimed design based on their contribution to visual appearance. (Page 22)

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of specification and prosecution history on claim scope
rubrics_metrics.description: The drawings are supplemented by the written description and the prosecution history may limit the claimed design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Insert case-specific descriptions of any limitations resulting from the description or prosecution history when applicable. (Page 19-22)

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement — compare accused design to the patent, not plaintiff’s product
rubrics_metrics.description: In deciding infringement you must compare the defendant’s accused product to the patent (the claimed design), not to the plaintiff’s commercial product, unless otherwise instructed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The accused product should be compared to the claimed design when making the infringement decision. (Page 23)

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct infringement — strict liability; proof standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct infringement occurs if the accused product incorporates the patented design or any colorable imitation thereof. Knowledge or intent to infringe is immaterial; direct infringement is a strict liability offense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plaintiff must prove direct infringement by a preponderance of the evidence (more likely than not). A defendant may directly infringe even if they believe in good faith they do not infringe. (Page 24-25)

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct infringement — ordinary observer/overall appearance test
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine infringement, compare the overall appearances of the accused design and the claimed design using the judge’s claim construction; if, in view of the prior art, the overall appearance of the accused design is substantially the same as the claimed design, find infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on the overall appearance, not individual features. Minor differences should not prevent a finding of infringement. Familiarize yourself with the prior art before making comparisons. (Page 25)

rubrics_metrics.name: Guidelines when prior art is similar
rubrics_metrics.description: When the claimed design is visually close to prior art, small differences between accused and claimed designs may be important; conspicuous inclusion of a claimed feature that departs from prior art may be important; if the accused design is closer to the claimed design than to the closest prior art, that may be important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are helpful guidelines but the sole test is whether the overall appearance of the accused design is substantially the same as the claimed design. (Page 25)

rubrics_metrics.name: Induced infringement — elements
rubrics_metrics.description: To show induced infringement the plaintiff must prove (1) someone has directly infringed the patent and (2) the defendant has actively and knowingly aided and abetted that direct infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plaintiff must show the defendant actually intended the acts that constitute direct infringement, knew of the patent, and knew or should have known that its actions would lead to infringement. Evidence may include advertising an infringing use or instructing how to engage in an infringing use. No direct infringement by the defendant is required so long as someone directly infringed. (Page 26)

rubrics_metrics.name: Contributory infringement — elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Contributory infringement exists if (1) someone directly infringed, and (2) the defendant sold, offered for sale, or imported a material component of the patented design that is not a staple article of commerce capable of substantial non-infringing use, with knowledge that the component was especially made or adapted for use in an infringing product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 'staple article of commerce' has substantial non-infringing uses that are not occasional, farfetched, impractical, experimental, or hypothetical. (Page 27)

rubrics_metrics.name: Willful infringement — two-step objective/subjective inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove willful infringement the plaintiff must persuade by clear and convincing evidence that the defendant was aware of the patent and that it is highly probable the defendant acted recklessly (objectively high likelihood of infringement), and then that the objectively-defined risk was known or so obvious it should have been known to the defendant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legitimate defenses demonstrate lack of recklessness. Consider factors such as: (1) whether defendant acted consistent with industry standards of commerce; (2) whether defendant intentionally copied without reasonable basis as distinguished from designing around; (3) whether defendant presented a substantial defense (including invalidity); and (4) if asserted, whether defendant relied on competent legal advice (opinion of counsel). Willfulness is relevant only to potential increased damages; jury should not consider willfulness when assessing damages unless instructed. (Page 28)

rubrics_metrics.name: Invalidity — burden and categories
rubrics_metrics.description: The defendant must prove by clear and convincing evidence that the asserted design patent(s) is/are invalid. Valid bases include: (a) anticipation by a single reference; (b) obviousness in view of multiple references; (c) on-sale or public use more than one year before filing; or (d) inequitable conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Insert defendant’s specific invalidity contentions for the case. (Page 29)

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and content of prior art for invalidity analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art includes designs/products publicly known or used in the U.S., patents/design registrations/publications dated more than one year before filing, public use/on-sale more than one year before filing, and any design made by others before the named inventors where not abandoned, suppressed, or concealed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the specific prior art items presented in the case. (Page 30)

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation — identical in all material respects
rubrics_metrics.description: A design is anticipated if a single prior art reference is 'identical in all material respects' to the overall visual impression of the claimed design; a design that is not new is anticipated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defendant must prove anticipation by clear and convincing evidence. Minor differences do not necessarily preclude anticipation, but the prior reference must be substantially the same in overall visual impression. (Page 31)

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation — public use and public display factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Public use more than one year before filing can bar patentability. Determine public use by totality of circumstances including nature of activities, public access/knowledge, and confidentiality obligations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public display (e.g., trade shows) is generally public use. Experimental use generally does not negate public use in design patents, though public display to gauge consumer opinion may be experimental when considering: length/number of tests, payment by users, secrecy agreements, records of tests, and whether others conducted experiments. (Page 31-32)

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation — offered for sale (on-sale bar)
rubrics_metrics.description: An inventor may not obtain a patent if the design was sold or offered for sale more than one year before filing; an offer to sell is an invitation to conclude a binding agreement and need not include price but requires a description of the goods and quantity terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To be 'on-sale' the sale/offer must have been primarily for profit rather than experimental purposes. Apply ordinary contract law principles (UCC) in assessing offers. (Page 33)

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation — prior design by another and inventorship
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent is anticipated if someone else created the patented design first. If inventorship is disputed, determine dates of conception, reduction to practice, and diligence; conception is proven by drawings/disclosure; reduction to practice occurs when an article embodying the design is produced or upon filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasonable diligence means continuous work toward reduction to practice, with ordinary interruptions allowed. Use case-specific means to show prior creation. (Page 34)

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness (design) — combination of references and Graham-like factors
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed design is invalid as obvious if a designer of ordinary skill would have combined a primary reference with a closely related secondary reference to create the same overall visual appearance as the claimed design. The primary reference must teach a specific design (not merely a concept).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate five factors: (1) scope and content of prior art relied on; (2) differences between claimed design and prior art; (3) level of ordinary skill in the art at the time; (4) whether the ordinary observer would find the two designs substantially the same; and (5) any additional considerations indicating obviousness or not. Defendant must prove obviousness by clear and convincing evidence. (Page 35-36)

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Different issues require different proof standards: infringement is decided by a preponderance of the evidence; invalidity (anticipation, obviousness, etc.) and willful infringement require proof by clear and convincing evidence (where specified).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the specified standards (preponderance vs clear and convincing) when evaluating evidence for each claim/defense. (Pages 24, 29, 28)

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordinary observer standard
rubrics_metrics.description: The jury serves as the panel of 'ordinary observers' for determining whether two designs are substantially the same for purposes of infringement and anticipation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When applying the ordinary observer test, consider the overall visual impression created by the designs, taking into account significant differences rather than trivial ones. (Pages 25, 31)
